does-per-creation-billing-cost-more-in-f.text:
← Patreon fee calculator

Does per-creation billing cost more in fees?

A per-creation pledge charges a patron once for every post you publish instead of once a month, so a $5-a-month supporter under per-creation billing might see four separate $1.25 charges in a busy month instead of one $5 charge. Same total pledge — but not the same fee bill, because payment processing charges a fixed fee on every charge, not on every dollar. On Patreon's Standard plan, the one every new page is on since August 2025, there is no small-charge discount to soften that at all.

Open the free payout calculator

The worked comparison: Standard plan

Take 100 patrons, each pledging $5 a month, on the Standard plan (10% platform fee, one flat processing rate regardless of charge size). The gross revenue is $500 either way. Here is what changes:

FigureMonthly billing (1 charge)Per-creation billing (4 posts, 4 charges)
Charge amount$5.00$1.25
Processing rate for that charge~2.9% + $0.30~2.9% + $0.30 (same — Standard has no small-charge rate)
Processing fee, this patron$0.445$1.345 (4 × $0.33625)
Total processing fees, 100 patrons$44.50$134.50
Platform fee (10% of $500 either way)$50.00$50.00
Total fees$94.50$184.50
Net payout$405.50$315.50

$90.00 less, from identical $500 gross revenue, purely from how the charge was split into four instead of one. The percentage portion of the fee is the same either way (2.9% of $500 is $14.50 total, whichever way it's charged); the entire gap is the $0.30 fixed fee, paid four times instead of once.

Does a legacy plan change this?

Partly. A legacy plan — a page created on or before August 4, 2025 — keeps its Lite/Pro/Premium platform fee and also gets a lower "micropayment" processing rate (about 5% + $0.10) on any charge under $3. On a Legacy Pro plan (8%), the identical 100-patron, $5-pledge, 4-post example pays $84.50 in total fees under monthly billing and $105.00 under per-creation billing — a $20.50 gap, much smaller than the Standard plan's $90.00, because the legacy rate's lower fixed fee ($0.10 instead of $0.30) partly offsets paying it four times. It is a real mitigant, not a myth — but it does not close the gap to zero.

When the gap closes

The gap shrinks as the per-post charge gets larger, on either plan, because the fixed fee stops dominating a bigger charge. A creator who posts once a month sees no split at all, since there is only one charge either way. The trap is specifically a low per-post amount multiplied by several posts in the same month — and it bites hardest on the Standard plan, which is what a page created today is on.

Use the calculator's plan, tier, and billing selectors to see this for your own pledge tiers and post cadence, rather than assuming either billing mode is always better.

Common questions

Does per-creation billing cost more in fees than monthly billing?

Often, yes, for the same total pledge. Payment processing charges a fixed fee every time a patron is charged, and per-creation billing charges more often for the same money. Splitting a $5 monthly pledge across 4 posts means four $1.25 charges instead of one $5 charge, and each of those four charges pays its own fixed fee -- on Patreon's Standard plan, with no small-charge discount, that fixed $0.30 is paid four times instead of once.

How much difference does that actually make on the Standard plan?

On 100 patrons at a $5 monthly pledge with the Standard plan's 10% platform fee, monthly billing pays $94.50 in total fees against $500 gross revenue, for a $405.50 net payout. The same $500 billed per-creation across 4 posts pays $184.50 in total fees, for a $315.50 net payout -- $90.00 less, from identical revenue, purely because of how the charge was split.

Does a legacy plan's micropayment rate change this?

It softens the gap but does not close it. A legacy plan (a page created on or before August 4, 2025) gets a lower processing rate -- about 5% plus a $0.10 fixed fee instead of the standard 2.9% plus $0.30 -- on any charge under $3. On a Legacy Pro plan (8% platform fee), the same 100-patron example pays $84.50 in total fees under monthly billing and $105.00 under per-creation billing -- a $20.50 gap, well below the Standard plan's $90.00 gap, because the legacy micropayment rate's lower fixed fee partly offsets charging four times instead of once.

Is per-creation billing always worse?

No. The gap shrinks as the per-post charge gets larger, because the fixed part of the fee stops dominating a bigger charge. A creator publishing once a month sees no split at all, since there is then only one charge either way. The trap is specifically low per-post amounts multiplied by several posts a month, and it is worse on the Standard plan than on a legacy plan because the Standard plan has no small-charge discount to soften it.

Why would a creator use per-creation billing at all, then?

It ties what a patron pays to how much the creator actually publishes that month, which some audiences find fairer than a flat monthly charge regardless of output. That is a real trade-off worth making deliberately -- this page is not an argument against per-creation billing, only against choosing it without seeing what it costs in fees for a given post cadence, pledge size, and plan.

Could Patreon's rates change and make this stale?

Yes. Patreon retired the three-tier plan for new creators in August 2025 in favor of the single Standard plan this page uses as its main example, and it publishes no live feed a static page could read. Treat this explainer as current as of the date on this page and verify anything material against your own Patreon creator dashboard and Patreon's own current help documentation.

FOR PATREON CREATORS

The pledge total isn't your payout. Take-home is.

Two fees come out of every pledge before it reaches you: your plan's platform fee (10% on Standard, or 5/8/12% on a legacy page), and a per-charge payment processing fee. Billing patrons "per creation" instead of monthly charges more often for the same money — and on the Standard plan, with no small-charge discount to soften it, that can cost a lot more in fees for identical revenue. This free calculator finds your real monthly payout and checks it against an income goal.

Billing per creation? See does per-creation billing cost more in fees? for the worked answer. Estimating in your head instead? See this calculator vs. doing the payout math yourself.

Have your whole member list instead of three typed tiers? The Patreon members churn analyzer reads your Members export and shows churn, declined-payment income at risk and fees — nothing uploaded.

Plan

The platform fee applies to your whole page, not per patron. Standard (10%) is what a page created after August 4, 2025 is on; a page from before that keeps its legacy Lite/Pro/Premium plan, which also gets a lower processing rate on any charge under $3. Verify your current plan on your own Patreon dashboard.

Pledge tiers

"Pledge" is what one charge costs a patron on that tier — the monthly amount under monthly billing, or the per-post amount under per-creation billing.

Billing & other income

"Posts this month" only changes the result under per-creation billing — that is how many times each patron is charged. "Other monthly income" is merch, tips, or income elsewhere — a figure you supply, added after fees since it never runs through Patreon's processing.

It does not model currency conversion (about 2.5% when a patron pays in a different currency than your payout currency), per-method payout fees, or any promotional rate — fold those into "other monthly income" as a negative adjustment if they apply to you. It never reads your Patreon account or replaces your own creator dashboard.

Private by default

There is no account. We count only anonymous local feature events (month-priced, gap-checked, link-copied, reset) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no patron counts, pledge amounts, or income figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Why is my real payout lower than the pledge total my dashboard shows?

Two fees come out before it reaches you. Patreon's platform fee is 10% on the Standard plan (pages created after August 4, 2025), or 5%/8%/12% (Lite/Pro/Premium) on a legacy plan that predates that change. On top of that, payment processing is charged per charge, not per patron or per month -- about 2.9% + $0.30 per charge on the Standard plan, always, regardless of size. A legacy plan pays that same standard rate too, except a charge under $3 instead pays a lower "micropayment" rate of about 5% + $0.10. Your dashboard's pledge total is before either fee.

Why does per-creation billing sometimes cost so much more in fees than monthly billing for the same total pledge?

Because payment processing charges a fixed fee every time a patron is charged, and per-creation billing charges more often for the same money. On the Standard plan, splitting a $5 monthly pledge into four $1.25 per-creation charges means paying the $0.30 fixed fee four times instead of once, with no micropayment discount to soften it -- this calculator's own worked comparison, at 100 patrons on that pledge, shows $94.50 in total fees under monthly billing versus $184.50 under per-creation billing, for identical $500 gross revenue.

Does a legacy plan's micropayment rate make per-creation billing cheaper?

It softens the gap but does not close it. A legacy plan's micropayment rate has a lower fixed fee ($0.10 instead of $0.30) for a charge under $3, so the same 100-patron, $5-pledge, 4-post example costs $105.00 in total fees under per-creation billing on a Legacy Pro plan -- $79.50 less than the Standard plan's $184.50, but still $20.50 more than that same plan's own $84.50 under monthly billing.

What is the micropayment rate and when does it apply?

It is a lower processing rate -- about 5% plus a $0.10 fixed fee instead of the standard roughly 2.9% plus $0.30 -- for any charge under $3, and it only exists on a legacy plan (a page created on or before August 4, 2025). Patreon's Standard plan, the one new pages are on today, charges the standard rate on every charge regardless of size, so a small per-creation charge gets no discount there at all.

Does this tool estimate ad revenue, one-time purchases, or shop sales?

No. This calculator prices recurring Patreon membership pledges only -- the three tier fields below. Merch sales, one-time tips, and income from other platforms are a single "other monthly income" figure you supply, added after fees since none of it runs through Patreon's processing.

Does anything about my numbers get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server and there is no account. Your inputs and target are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button below.

vs-doing-the-math-yourself.html.text:
← Patreon fee calculator

Patreon fee calculator vs. doing the payout math yourself

The quick mental estimate most creators reach for is "gross pledges times (1 minus the platform fee)" -- $1,400 pledged, 10% platform fee, so about $1,260 lands in the bank. That estimate is not wrong about the platform fee. It is wrong about the other fee: payment processing charges a fixed dollar amount on every charge, not a share of revenue, and a percentage-only estimate has nowhere to put a fixed dollar amount. On the calculator's own default scenario, that gap is $139.60 -- real money, and it does not show up until you count charges instead of dollars.

Open the free payout calculator

The worked comparison

Take the calculator's own defaults: 200 patrons at $3, 100 patrons at $5, and 30 patrons at $10, all billed monthly on the Standard plan (10% platform fee, ~2.9% + $0.30 processing on every charge). Gross pledge revenue is $1,400.00, across 330 total charges (200 + 100 + 30 -- one charge per patron under monthly billing). Here is what a flat-percentage mental estimate gets wrong:

FigureMental estimate (gross × 90%)Actual (calculator)
Gross pledge revenue$1,400.00$1,400.00
Platform fee (10%)$140.00$140.00
Processing feesnot counted$139.60 (330 charges × ~2.9% + $0.30 each)
Total fees$140.00$279.60
Net payout$1,260.00$1,120.40
Effective take-home rate90.0%80.0%

$139.60 too high, on identical gross revenue -- a 12.5% overestimate of the actual net payout. Of the $139.60 in processing fees the estimate missed entirely, $99.00 is the fixed $0.30 fee charged 330 times (71% of the processing bill), and only the remaining $40.60 is the 2.9% percentage rate a "roughly 3%" mental adjustment might have caught.

Why revenue alone does not predict the gap

Two creators with the same $1,400 gross pledge revenue can owe very different processing fees, because the fixed fee scales with charge count, not with dollars. A creator with 330 small pledges pays that $0.30 fixed fee 330 times; a creator with the same $1,400 total spread across a handful of large pledges pays it only a handful of times. A percentage-of-revenue mental estimate cannot see the difference, because it never looks at how many charges produced the revenue. Billing frequency compounds the same trap -- switching from monthly to per-creation billing multiplies the charge count for the same pledge total, which the calculator's own per-creation-billing guide works through in detail.

When mental math is close enough

The gap shrinks toward zero as the average charge size grows, because a fixed $0.30 fee is a rounding error against a $500 charge and a real bite against a $3 one. A creator with a few large pledges and monthly billing will find a flat-percentage estimate reasonably close. The trap is specifically many small pledges, a legacy plan's under-$3 micropayment charges, or per-creation billing splitting one pledge into several charges a month -- exactly the shape the calculator's tier and billing inputs are built to catch.

Common questions

Why does subtracting just the platform fee percentage overstate the payout?

Because payment processing charges a fixed fee (about $0.30 on the Standard plan) on every charge, not a percentage of revenue, and a percentage-only mental estimate has no place to put a fixed dollar amount. On the calculator's own default scenario -- 200 patrons at $3, 100 at $5, and 30 at $10, all billed monthly on the Standard plan -- 330 charges each carry that fixed fee, for $99.00 that a flat 10% deduction never accounts for.

How big is the gap in dollars?

On that same default scenario, subtracting only the 10% platform fee from $1,400.00 gross gives $1,260.00. The calculator's actual net payout, after both the platform fee and processing fees, is $1,120.40 -- a $139.60 overestimate, or about 12.5% too high.

Does the gap depend on patron count and pledge size, or just total revenue?

It depends on how many charges the total revenue is split across, which total revenue alone does not tell you. Two creators with identical $1,400 gross pledge revenue can have very different processing-fee bills if one has many small pledges (more charges) and the other has fewer, larger ones (fewer charges) -- a percentage-of-revenue estimate treats them as identical when they are not.

Is the fixed fee the whole gap, or does the percentage matter too?

Both apply, but the fixed fee is the larger and more easily forgotten part. In the default scenario, processing fees total $139.60: $99.00 of that is the fixed $0.30 charged 330 times, and the remaining $40.60 is the 2.9% processing rate applied to $1,400 of revenue. A mental estimate that remembers "there's a processing fee, roughly 3%" still misses the $99.00 fixed portion -- 71% of the true processing-fee bill.

When is a quick mental estimate close enough?

When you have very few, very large pledges, so the fixed per-charge fee is a rounding error next to the percentage fee -- one $500 pledge on the Standard plan pays $14.80 in processing (2.9% plus one $0.30 fixed fee), close to a flat percentage guess. The trap grows with patron count and shrinks with average pledge size, and per-creation billing (charging once per post instead of once a month) multiplies the charge count further -- see the calculator's own per-creation-billing guide for that case.

Could Patreon's fee structure change and make this comparison stale?

Yes. Patreon retired the three-tier legacy plan for new creators in August 2025 in favor of a single Standard plan, and it publishes no live feed a static page could read.
